choices.text: Torsion of the penis

explanation.summary: Hypospadias is classified by meatal location along the ventral penis; penoscrotal, scrotal, and perineal openings are proximal forms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypospadias is classified based on the location of the urethral opening along the ventral penis, ranging from distal (glanular, subcoronal) to proximal (penoscrotal, scrotal, perineal) positions. An opening at the penoscrotal junction is therefore a proximal hypospadias, which reflects greater anatomic and clinical severity along this spectrum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Distal forms are the glanular and subcoronal positions near the glans, not the penoscrotal junction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epispadias places the urethral opening on the dorsal surface of the penis, not the ventral surface.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A glanular opening sits on the glans itself, the most distal position in the classification.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Torsion of the penis is an apparent malrotation of the glans, not a malposition of the urethral meatus.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man reports progressively worsening curvature of the penis with erections over the past year. Examination shows a firm plaque along the shaft; the urethral meatus is at the tip of the glans, and he reports no penile abnormalities earlier in life. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chordee

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epispadias

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypospadias

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peyronie disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Torsion of the penis

explanation.summary: Peyronie disease is an acquired adult condition of fibrous plaques in the erectile tissues causing progressive curvature, unlike chordee, which is present from birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: New, progressive penile curvature in adulthood with a palpable fibrous plaque in the erectile tissue is characteristic of Peyronie disease. Its acquired onset distinguishes it from chordee, the congenital ventral curvature caused by abnormal ventral tissue development that accompanies hypospadias and is present from birth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chordee is present from birth; this man's curvature began in adulthood and is associated with a plaque.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epispadias places the meatus on the dorsal penile surface, which is not present here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: In hypospadias the urethral meatus lies on the ventral penis; this patient's meatus is normally positioned at the glans tip.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penile torsion is a congenital apparent malrotation of the glans, not an acquired curvature with plaque formation.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A newborn boy with hypospadias has a foreskin with a hooded, 'cobra-head' appearance that leaves the glans exposed. Which of the following abnormalities of foreskin development best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent dorsal foreskin with redundant ventral foreskin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absent ventral foreskin with redundant dorsal foreskin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Circumferential absence of the foreskin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Circumferential redundancy of the foreskin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fibrous plaque formation within the foreskin

explanation.summary: The hooded foreskin of hypospadias results from absent ventral foreskin combined with redundant dorsal foreskin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally the foreskin covers the glans circumferentially. In hypospadias, the ventral foreskin is absent while the dorsal foreskin is redundant, leaving the glans exposed and creating the characteristic dorsal hood or cobra-head appearance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The deficiency is ventral and the redundancy dorsal, matching the ventral fusion defect of hypospadias; the reverse pattern is not described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The foreskin is not absent all the way around; dorsal tissue is present and redundant, forming the hood.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Uniform excess foreskin would cover the glans circumferentially rather than leaving it exposed with a dorsal hood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fibrous plaques occur in the erectile tissues in Peyronie disease, an acquired adult condition unrelated to foreskin development.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with uncorrected hypospadias requires urinary catheterization before an unrelated operation. The nurse reports that the catheter repeatedly stops after advancing a short distance into an opening at the tip of the glans. Which of the following best explains this difficulty?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A fibrous plaque narrowing the distal urethra

choices.label: B
choices.text: A urethral meatus located on the dorsal shaft

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compression of the urethra by hydrocele fluid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Malrotation of the glans obstructing the meatus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage of the catheter into a blind-ending urethral pit

explanation.summary: Adults with uncorrected hypospadias may have a blind-ending urethral pit that misleads catheter placement or urethral instrumentation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In adult males with uncorrected hypospadias, a urethral pit — a blind-ending urethral opening — may be present at the expected meatal position and can be misleading at the time of catheter placement or urethral instrumentation. The functional meatus actually lies along the ventral penis, so the catheter entering the pit stops after a short distance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A fibrous plaque in the erectile tissue characterizes Peyronie disease and causes curvature, not a short blind passage at the glans.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A dorsal meatus defines epispadias; this patient has hypospadias, with the true opening on the ventral surface.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A hydrocele is fluid within the tunica vaginalis around the testis and does not obstruct urethral catheterization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penile torsion is an apparent malrotation of the glans and is not described as blocking passage of a catheter.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common congenital anomaly of the penis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chordee

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congenital absence of the vas deferens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epispadias

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypospadias

choices.label: E
choices.text: Torsion of the penis

explanation.summary: Hypospadias, from incomplete ventral fusion of the urethral folds, is the most common congenital anomaly of the penis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypospadias is the most common congenital anomaly of the penis and reflects abnormal fusion of the urethral folds, placing the urethral opening along the ventral surface rather than at the tip of the glans. Surgical correction is typically recommended because abnormal urethral anatomy can interfere with urination and future reproductive function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chordee is a ventral curvature often associated with hypospadias rather than the most common anomaly itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Congenital absence of the vas deferens is an anomaly of the sperm-transport ducts, not of the penis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epispadias is much less common than hypospadias and arises from abnormal dorsal positioning of the genital tubercle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Penile torsion is an associated finding of apparent glans malrotation, not the most common penile anomaly.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A newborn boy has a urethral opening on the dorsal surface of the penis, and the bladder mucosa is exposed on the anterior abdominal wall. Abnormal development of which of the following best explains the urethral finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Descent of the testes through the inguinal canal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of the vas deferens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fusion of the urethral folds along the ventral midline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obliteration of the processus vaginalis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Positioning of the genital tubercle

explanation.summary: Epispadias results from an abnormally dorsal position of the genital tubercle, which alters formation of the penile urethra.
explanation.whyCorrect: A dorsal urethral opening defines epispadias, which occurs when the genital tubercle develops in an abnormally dorsal position rather than from failed urethral fold fusion. The accompanying bladder exstrophy reflects the more extensive disruption of midline development frequently associated with epispadias, and surgical correction is typically required.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failure of testicular descent causes cryptorchidism with an empty scrotum, unrelated to the urethral opening.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Abnormal vas deferens formation causes obstructive azoospermia in adulthood and does not affect the urethral meatus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure of ventral urethral fold fusion causes hypospadias, in which the opening lies on the ventral surface.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failed obliteration of the processus vaginalis causes a communicating hydrocele, not a urethral malposition.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens and obstructive azoospermia asks whether he can have biological children. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Biological fatherhood is not possible; donor sperm is required

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intrauterine insemination with his ejaculated semen is effective

choices.label: C
choices.text: Natural conception is likely because spermatogenesis is preserved

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sperm retrieval combined with IVF or ICSI can allow fatherhood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Testosterone therapy can restore sperm to the ejaculate

explanation.summary: In CBAVD, spermatogenesis is normal, so sperm retrieval combined with IVF or ICSI can allow men to father biological children.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although natural conception is generally not possible in CBAVD because sperm cannot be transported into the semen, spermatogenesis within the testes is normal. Assisted reproductive technologies — sperm retrieval combined with in vitro fertilization or intracytoplasmic sperm injection — can therefore allow affected men to father biological children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Donor sperm is not the only option, since the patient's own sperm can be retrieved for IVF or ICSI.
whyWrongByChoice.B: His ejaculate contains no sperm (azoospermia), so insemination with ejaculated semen cannot succeed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Preserved spermatogenesis does not permit natural conception, because absent vasa prevent sperm from reaching the semen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hormone levels are normal in this condition; the problem is ductal absence, which testosterone cannot correct.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens is found to carry CFTR mutations. He and his partner plan to pursue sperm retrieval with intracytoplasmic sperm injection. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation before proceeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetic counseling for the couple

choices.label: B
choices.text: Karyotype analysis of the patient

choices.label: C
choices.text: Measurement of serum testosterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scrotal ultrasonography to assess testicular size

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequencing of the androgen receptor gene

explanation.summary: Genetic counseling is recommended for CBAVD, especially when CFTR mutations are present, to assess the risk of transmitting cystic fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because CBAVD is linked to CFTR mutations, genetic counseling is recommended — especially when CFTR mutations are identified — to assess the risk of passing cystic fibrosis or related conditions to offspring conceived through assisted reproduction. Emotional support and counseling may also help with the psychological impact of infertility.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The condition arises from CFTR mutations, not a chromosomal abnormality, so karyotyping does not address the transmission risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Testosterone is characteristically normal in CBAVD and would not change reproductive planning.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Testicular size is normal in this condition, and imaging adds nothing to assessing the genetic risk to offspring.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Androgen receptor sequencing evaluates androgen insensitivity or Kennedy disease, which are not suggested in a normally virilized man with CBAVD.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man undergoing an infertility evaluation is found to have congenital absence of the vas deferens on the left side only; the right vas deferens is palpable and normal. CFTR mutation testing is negative. Which of the following associated anomalies is most likely in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bilateral cryptorchidism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bladder exstrophy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Communicating hydrocele

choices.label: D
choices.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unilateral renal agenesis

explanation.summary: A subset of congenital absence of the vas deferens not explained by CFTR is associated with unilateral renal agenesis and other urinary tract anomalies.
explanation.whyCorrect: A smaller subset of congenital absence of the vas deferens is associated with unilateral renal agenesis, and the genetic basis of this form is less well understood than the CFTR-related form. Other structural anomalies of the urinary tract may also be present. Unilateral absence (CUAVD) may not significantly affect fertility, in contrast to bilateral absence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryptorchidism reflects failed testicular descent and is linked to prematurity, not to absence of the vas deferens.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bladder exstrophy is associated with epispadias and failed midline abdominal closure, not with vasal agenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A communicating hydrocele results from a patent processus vaginalis and has no described association with vasal agenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia causes disorders of sexual development through abnormal steroid synthesis, not isolated vasal absence.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A newborn has ambiguous external genitalia. Gonadal biopsy shows both ovarian follicles and seminiferous tubules within the same individual. The disorder in this newborn results from a disruption at which of the following levels of sexual development?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Closure of embryonic peritoneal connections

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fusion of the urethral folds

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gonadal differentiation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hormone action at target tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hormone production by the adrenal glands

explanation.summary: Ovotesticular DSD, with both ovarian and testicular tissue in one individual, is a problem of gonadal differentiation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The presence of both ovarian and testicular tissue defines ovotesticular DSD, which is a problem with gonadal differentiation — one of the three levels at which DSDs arise (chromosomal or gonadal development, hormone production, and hormone action). The most common karyotype is 46,XX, the gonadal tissue is often nonfunctional, and the external genitalia may appear female, male, or ambiguous depending on hormonal influence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failure of processus vaginalis closure causes hydroceles and inguinal hernia risk, not mixed gonadal tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Abnormal urethral fold fusion causes hypospadias, an anomaly of the penile urethra rather than of gonadal development.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective hormone action at target tissues describes androgen insensitivity syndrome, in which the gonads are testes only.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Excess adrenal androgen production underlies 46,XX DSD from congenital adrenal hyperplasia, in which the gonads are normal ovaries.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man presents with several years of progressive muscle weakness. Examination shows gynecomastia, and he and his partner have been unable to conceive. A diagnosis of spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy is made. Which of the following best describes the underlying genetic abnormality?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete deletion of the androgen receptor gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disrupted gonadal differentiation with ovotesticular tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enzymatic deficiency of adrenal 21-hydroxylase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss-of-function mutation of the CFTR chloride channel gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trinucleotide repeat expansion in the androgen receptor gene

explanation.summary: Kennedy disease is an X-linked trinucleotide repeat disorder of the androgen receptor producing adult-onset weakness, gynecomastia, and infertility from partial androgen insensitivity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Kennedy disease (spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy) is an X-linked trinucleotide repeat disorder of the androgen receptor. It presents in adulthood with progressive muscle weakness, gynecomastia, and infertility, findings that reflect partial androgen insensitivity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Kennedy disease results from a repeat expansion within the androgen receptor gene, producing partial rather than complete loss of androgen signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ovotesticular DSD is a congenital disorder of gonadal differentiation, not an adult-onset neuromuscular disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia with virilization of a 46,XX fetus, presenting at birth rather than in adulthood.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CFTR mutations cause congenital absence of the vas deferens with obstructive azoospermia, not progressive weakness with gynecomastia.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A newborn with a 46,XY karyotype has ambiguous external genitalia. Imaging identifies testes in the inguinal region, and the serum testosterone concentration is low for age. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 21-hydroxylase deficiency causing marked adrenal androgen excess

choices.label: B
choices.text: A form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia impairing testosterone synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: CFTR-related bilateral degeneration of the mesonephric duct derivatives in utero

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss-of-function mutation of the androgen receptor in target tissues

choices.label: E
choices.text: Presence of both ovarian and testicular tissue within the same gonad

explanation.summary: In 46,XY individuals, under-virilization can result from defects in androgen production; rare forms of CAH impair testosterone synthesis and cause ambiguous or female external genitalia at birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under-virilization of a 46,XY individual can arise from defects in androgen production or androgen action. The low testosterone here points to a production defect: rare forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia impair testosterone synthesis, leading to ambiguous or female external genitalia at birth despite the presence of testes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 21-hydroxylase deficiency raises androgen production, which virilizes a 46,XX fetus; it does not explain an under-virilized 46,XY newborn with low testosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CFTR-related loss of the vas deferens causes obstructive azoospermia in normally virilized adult men, not ambiguous genitalia at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: In androgen insensitivity syndrome the testes produce testosterone, so levels are not low; the defect is failure of target tissues to respond.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ovotesticular DSD requires both ovarian and testicular tissue and is most often 46,XX; imaging here shows testes.

questions.topicName: Congenital Disorders of the Reproductive Systems

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman who never received routine childhood vaccinations develops fever, headache, lymphadenopathy, and a diffuse erythematous rash; serologic testing confirms rubella. Several weeks later she is found to be pregnant, with the infection estimated to have occurred very early in gestation. The fetus is at greatest risk for which of the following patterns of congenital anomalies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and heart defects

choices.label: B
choices.text: Limb reduction defects of the upper extremities

choices.label: C
choices.text: Microcephaly with intracranial calcifications

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neural tube defects of the lumbosacral spine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and joint anomalies

explanation.summary: Congenital rubella causes cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rubella is a TORCHeS pathogen that crosses the placenta even when maternal illness is mild. Infection in very early pregnancy carries a high risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, and the classic triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart defects, along with developmental delay.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Limb reduction defects (phocomelia) are the hallmark of thalidomide exposure, a chemical teratogen rather than an infectious one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Microcephaly with intracranial calcifications, hearing loss, and vision impairment is the classic pattern of congenital CMV infection, not rubella.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neural tube defects are associated with valproic acid exposure and folate deficiency, not with rubella infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and joint anomalies characterize fetal alcohol syndrome, not congenital rubella.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is exposed to a known chemical teratogen during week 6 of gestation. Compared with exposure at other times in pregnancy, exposure during this period places the embryo at highest risk for which of the following outcomes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Isolated functional deficits without structural change

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of the embryo or no lasting effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Major structural anomalies of developing organs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minor structural changes in fully formed organs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Postnatal growth failure without congenital anomalies

explanation.summary: Weeks 3-8 are the most teratogen-sensitive period because organogenesis is occurring.
explanation.whyCorrect: During weeks 3-8, all major body structures are forming (organogenesis), making this the most sensitive window for teratogenic injury. Exposure during this period can produce major structural anomalies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Functional deficits without major structural change are more typical of the fetal period (weeks 9-38), after organogenesis is largely complete.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An all-or-none effect (embryo loss or no lasting effect) describes exposure during weeks 1-2, before significant differentiation has occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Minor structural changes are characteristic of exposure during weeks 9-38, when organogenesis is largely finished.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Postnatal growth failure alone is not the characteristic risk of exposure during organogenesis, which threatens major structural development.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman unknowingly takes a teratogenic medication 10 days after fertilization, before significant embryonic differentiation has occurred. Which of the following best describes the expected effect of this exposure on the conceptus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disorganized cellular architecture in a single tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Either loss of the embryo or no lasting effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: Functional deficits that appear only after birth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Major structural anomalies of multiple organ systems

choices.label: E
choices.text: Minor anomalies limited to one organ system

explanation.summary: Teratogen exposure in weeks 1-2 produces an all-or-none effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the embryo has not yet undergone significant differentiation during weeks 1-2, a teratogenic insult in this window either kills the embryo or leaves no lasting effect. This is the classic all-or-none phenomenon.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Disorganized cellular architecture describes dysplasia, an intrinsic genetic abnormality of tissue organization, not the effect of very early teratogen exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Functional deficits characterize later fetal exposure; the pre-differentiation embryo instead shows an all-or-none response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Major structural anomalies result from exposure during weeks 3-8, when organogenesis is under way, not before differentiation begins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Minor structural anomalies are typical of exposure in the fetal period (weeks 9-38), not the first two weeks.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy becomes pregnant while taking a medication for seizure prophylaxis. Her fetus is subsequently found to have a neural tube defect. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this anomaly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Constriction of the embryo by amniotic bands

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct DNA strand breaks in embryonic cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disruption of maternal-fetal folate metabolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fetal hyperglycemia with oxidative stress

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasoconstriction of placental blood vessels

explanation.summary: Valproic acid raises neural tube defect risk by disrupting folate metabolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Valproic acid, used for seizure prophylaxis and mood stabilization, disrupts folate metabolism. Because folate supports DNA synthesis and methylation needed for neural tube closure, this disruption increases the risk of neural tube defects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amniotic bands cause disruption through mechanical constriction of limbs or digits, not neural tube defects from a medication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA breaks in rapidly dividing cells describe the injury caused by ionizing radiation, a physical rather than chemical teratogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fetal hyperglycemia and oxidative stress are the mechanism by which poorly controlled maternal diabetes injures the fetus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Placental vasoconstriction is the mechanism of cocaine, which causes low birth weight and prematurity rather than neural tube defects.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with bipolar disorder has been maintained on a mood-stabilizing medication throughout an unplanned pregnancy. Fetal echocardiography is performed because her medication is classically associated with which of the following anomalies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cataracts with sensorineural deafness

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleft palate with skeletal defects

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve

choices.label: D
choices.text: Limb reduction defect of both arms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neural tube defect of the lumbar spine

explanation.summary: Lithium is classically associated with Ebstein anomaly, a tricuspid valve malformation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lithium, used to treat bipolar disorder, is associated with Ebstein anomaly, a malformation of the tricuspid valve. Although the association is weaker than initially reported, it remains a board-tested link that prompts fetal cardiac evaluation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cataracts and sensorineural deafness are features of congenital rubella infection, not a medication effect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cleft palate with skeletal and visceral defects is described with high-dose ionizing radiation exposure, not lithium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Limb reduction defects are the hallmark of thalidomide, historically used as a sedative and anti-nausea drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neural tube defects are linked to valproic acid, which disrupts folate metabolism; valproate is a mood stabilizer but the classic cardiac link here is lithium's.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is evaluated for developmental delay. Examination shows growth restriction, a smooth philtrum, a thin upper lip, joint anomalies, and a ventricular septal defect. Prenatal exposure to which of the following most likely explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heavy maternal cigarette smoking in pregnancy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Repeated maternal cocaine use in pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Poorly controlled maternal diabetes mellitus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Significant maternal alcohol ingestion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Untreated maternal phenylketonuria (PKU)

explanation.summary: Fetal alcohol syndrome causes growth restriction, intellectual disability, characteristic facies, joint anomalies, and heart defects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Significant alcohol ingestion during pregnancy can cause fetal alcohol syndrome, characterized by growth restriction, intellectual disability, joint anomalies, congenital heart defects, and characteristic facial features including a smooth philtrum and thin upper lip.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Smoking is associated with low birth weight and preterm labor from impaired placental blood flow, not this facial phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cocaine causes placental vasoconstriction leading to low birth weight, prematurity, and subtle cognitive deficits, without the characteristic FAS facies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Maternal diabetes causes nervous system, skeletal, and heart anomalies through fetal hyperglycemia, but not the smooth philtrum and thin upper lip.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Maternal PKU causes intellectual disability, heart defects, and growth restriction via high phenylalanine, but lacks the distinctive facial features described here.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman diagnosed with phenylketonuria in infancy stopped following her restricted diet years ago. She is now pregnant. Which of the following best explains how her condition threatens the fetus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A pathogen crosses the placenta despite mild maternal illness

choices.label: B
choices.text: An inherited enzyme defect is transmitted to the fetus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated maternal phenylalanine acts as a metabolic teratogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal hyperglycemia produces fetal oxidative stress

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced amniotic fluid compresses normally formed structures

explanation.summary: In maternal PKU, high phenylalanine crosses the placenta and acts as a metabolic teratogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: In maternal PKU, high maternal phenylalanine levels cross the placenta and act as a metabolic teratogen. Elevated phenylalanine in fetal blood can cause intellectual disability, heart defects, and intrauterine growth restriction, which is why newborn PKU screening enables dietary counseling before future pregnancies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transplacental pathogen passage describes infectious teratogens such as the TORCHeS organisms, not a maternal metabolic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The fetal risk in maternal PKU comes from exposure to the mother's elevated phenylalanine, not from the fetus inheriting the enzyme defect itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fetal hyperglycemia with oxidative stress is the mechanism of injury in poorly controlled maternal diabetes mellitus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oligohydramnios causing compression describes the mechanism of deformations such as clubfoot, not maternal PKU.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A newborn is delivered with constriction rings around the right forearm and amputation of two fingers. Torn strands of amniotic tissue are found wrapped around the affected limb. The digits had been developing normally before becoming entangled. This anomaly is best classified as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deformation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disruption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dysplasia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Malformation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Syndrome

explanation.summary: Amniotic band injury is the classic disruption: an extrinsic force damages a normally developing structure.
explanation.whyCorrect: A disruption results from extrinsic breakdown or interference with a structure that was developing normally. Amniotic bands wrapping around fetal limbs or digits cause constriction, ischemia, or amputation, making them the classic example of this mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A deformation is caused by mechanical forces that alter shape or position while the tissue remains intact; amniotic bands destroy tissue rather than merely reshaping it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dysplasia is an intrinsic abnormality of cellular organization within a tissue, not damage from an external structure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A malformation arises from an intrinsically abnormal developmental program; here the digits were forming normally until the bands injured them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A syndrome is a group of anomalies sharing one underlying cause, not a single mechanical injury to one limb.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A newborn twin is noted to have clubfoot. The pregnancy was complicated by oligohydramnios, and imaging during gestation showed persistent pressure of the fetus against the uterine wall. The affected foot has structurally intact, normally formed tissues. Which of the following best classifies this anomaly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Association

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deformation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disruption

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dysplasia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Malformation

explanation.summary: Clubfoot from uterine compression is a deformation: mechanical force reshaping an intact, normally developing structure.
explanation.whyCorrect: A deformation is caused by external mechanical forces acting on a normally developing structure; the tissue is intact and only its shape or position is altered. Oligohydramnios and crowding from multiple gestation produce persistent pressure that can cause clubfoot or retrognathia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An association is a pattern of multiple co-occurring anomalies without a unifying cause, not a single pressure-related defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A disruption involves destruction or interruption of a developing structure by an outside force; here the tissue is intact, not damaged.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dysplasia is disorganized cellular architecture from an intrinsic genetic abnormality, not a positional change from compression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A malformation reflects an intrinsically abnormal developmental process, but this foot formed normally and was reshaped by pressure.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: An infant is evaluated for disproportionately short limbs and other features of dwarfism. Genetic testing identifies a mutation in FGFR3 that impairs endochondral ossification by altering cell growth and signaling within developing cartilage. This condition is best classified as which type of error in morphogenesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Association of sporadic skeletal findings

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deformation from mechanical compression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disruption of a normally forming skeleton

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dysplasia with disorganized cellular architecture

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequence initiated by a single skeletal defect

explanation.summary: Achondroplasia, from an FGFR3 mutation, is the most common skeletal dysplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dysplasia is an intrinsic developmental abnormality characterized by disorganized cell structure within a tissue, typically arising from mutations that alter cell growth, differentiation, or signaling. Achondroplasia, caused by an FGFR3 mutation that impairs endochondral ossification, is the classic and most common skeletal dysplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An association describes co-occurring anomalies without an identified unifying cause; achondroplasia has a defined single-gene cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Deformations result from external mechanical forces such as uterine compression, not from a genetic defect in tissue organization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Disruptions require an extrinsic force damaging a normally developing structure; achondroplasia is intrinsic and genetic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A sequence is a cascade of multiple anomalies from one initiating event, not a single tissue-level abnormality of cartilage.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A stillborn infant has pulmonary hypoplasia, limb positioning abnormalities, and flattened facial features. Autopsy reveals a severe primary abnormality of the urinary system that had caused markedly reduced urine production and oligohydramnios. Which of the following best explains why these anomalies are classified as a sequence rather than a syndrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All the anomalies share one underlying chromosomal abnormality

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least three hallmark features were required for the diagnosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each anomaly resulted from a cascade begun by a single initiating defect

choices.label: D
choices.text: The anomalies are parallel manifestations of one teratogenic exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: The findings co-occur more often than expected without a known cause

explanation.summary: A sequence is a cascade of anomalies all stemming from a single initiating event, as in Potter sequence.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Potter sequence, a primary urinary abnormality severely reduces urine production, causing oligohydramnios, which in turn produces pulmonary hypoplasia and compression deformities such as limb positioning abnormalities and flattened facies. Because each abnormality leads to the next, the pattern is a sequence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A shared chromosomal abnormality producing parallel anomalies defines a syndrome, such as Down syndrome from trisomy 21.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A minimum of three hallmark features is the diagnostic criterion for VACTERL association, not the definition of a sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parallel manifestations of a single etiologic event, including a teratogenic exposure, describe a syndrome rather than a cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Findings that co-occur more often than expected without a unifying cause define an association, such as VACTERL.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A newborn girl has a coloboma, a congenital heart defect, choanal atresia, growth retardation, genital anomalies, and ear abnormalities with deafness. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this pattern of anomalies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activating mutation in the FGFR3 gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mutation in the RET proto-oncogene

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recessive mutation in the NECTIN1 gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sporadic mutation in the CHD7 gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trisomy of chromosome 21

explanation.summary: CHARGE syndrome is a usually sporadic genetic disorder caused by CHD7 mutations.
explanation.whyCorrect: The findings spell out CHARGE syndrome: Coloboma, Heart defects, choanal Atresia, growth Retardation, Genital anomalies, and Ear abnormalities with deafness. CHARGE is a usually sporadic syndrome caused by mutations in the CHD7 gene, with the anomalies representing parallel manifestations of that single genetic cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FGFR3 mutation causes achondroplasia, a skeletal dysplasia with impaired endochondral ossification and dwarfism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: RET mutations impair enteric neural crest migration and cause Hirschsprung disease with absent colonic ganglion cells and severe constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NECTIN1 mutations cause the autosomal recessive Cleft Lip/Palate-Ectodermal Dysplasia Syndrome, not this constellation of findings.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trisomy 21 causes Down syndrome, with intellectual disability, characteristic facies, and heart defects, but not coloboma or choanal atresia.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: At a preconception counseling visit, a couple asks how common serious birth defects are. In the United States, approximately what percentage of live births are diagnosed with a major structural congenital anomaly at birth?

explanation.summary: Major structural anomalies are diagnosed in about 3% of live births in the United States.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the United States, major structural anomalies are diagnosed in about 3% of live births. Additional anomalies identified later in childhood raise the cumulative incidence to around 8% by age 5.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 0.3% substantially underestimates the birth prevalence of major structural anomalies, which is about tenfold higher.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 8% is the cumulative incidence by age 5, after anomalies not apparent at birth have been identified, not the rate at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: About 20% is the proportion of congenital anomalies that have an identifiable cause, not the birth prevalence of anomalies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 80% is the proportion of congenital anomalies with no currently known cause, not the frequency of anomalies among live births.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A genetics clinic reviews the etiologies of structural congenital anomalies in its patient population. Which of the following statements about the causes of congenital anomalies is accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 80% of anomalies have a single well-defined cause

choices.label: B
choices.text: Extrinsic teratogens account for the majority of all anomalies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intrinsic genetic factors account for about 12-19% of anomalies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multifactorial influences have been excluded in unexplained cases

choices.label: E
choices.text: Teratogens cause more anomalies than genetic factors do

explanation.summary: Genetic factors cause 12-19% of anomalies, teratogens 1-8%, and about 80% have no known cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among cases with known causes, intrinsic genetic factors, including chromosomal abnormalities and gene mutations, account for 12-19% of anomalies, while extrinsic environmental factors (teratogens) account for 1-8%. These genetic conditions may follow autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, X-linked, or mitochondrial inheritance patterns.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only about 20% of congenital anomalies have an identifiable cause; the remaining 80% do not.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Teratogens account for only 1-8% of anomalies; most anomalies have no identifiable cause at all.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A substantial proportion of the 80% of anomalies without a known cause are thought to be multifactorial, combining genetic and environmental influences.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genetic factors (12-19%) account for a larger share of anomalies than teratogens (1-8%), not the reverse.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: An infant of consanguineous parents is born with cleft lip and palate together with ectodermal dysplasia. Genetic testing identifies biallelic mutations in NECTIN1, consistent with an autosomal recessive disorder. The developmental defect most likely results from impaired function of which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A cell adhesion molecule required for adherens junctions

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chromatin regulator mutated in a sporadic multi-anomaly syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: A folate-dependent pathway supporting DNA methylation

choices.label: D
choices.text: A proto-oncogene guiding enteric neural crest migration

choices.label: E
choices.text: A receptor kinase that drives endochondral ossification

explanation.summary: NECTIN1 encodes a cell adhesion molecule essential for adherens junctions and epithelial integrity; its loss causes CLPED1.
explanation.whyCorrect: NECTIN1 encodes a cell adhesion molecule essential for adherens junctions and epithelial integrity. Mutations in this gene are linked to Cleft Lip/Palate-Ectodermal Dysplasia Syndrome (CLPED1), an autosomal recessive disorder, illustrating how a single phenotype such as cleft lip can arise from a defined genetic cause.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CHD7 mutations cause CHARGE syndrome, with coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, growth retardation, and genital and ear anomalies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Disrupted folate metabolism, as with valproic acid exposure, raises the risk of neural tube defects rather than causing this adhesion-molecule disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RET proto-oncogene mutations impair migration of enteric neural crest cells, causing Hirschsprung disease, not this craniofacial disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Impaired endochondral ossification from an FGFR3 mutation causes achondroplasia, a skeletal dysplasia, not cleft lip/palate with ectodermal dysplasia.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A newborn has nonsyndromic cleft lip with palate. There is no family history of a single-gene disorder, but the mother smoked cigarettes throughout pregnancy, and genome-wide association studies have linked this anomaly to at least 26 genetic loci. The etiology of this anomaly is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chromosomal abnormality such as a trisomy

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mechanical deformation from intrauterine pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single-gene autosomal recessive disorder in every case

choices.label: D
choices.text: An exclusively environmental effect of tobacco smoke

choices.label: E
choices.text: Multifactorial, combining genetic and environmental influences

explanation.summary: Nonsyndromic cleft lip with palate reflects combined genetic and environmental influences.
explanation.whyCorrect: A single phenotype can arise from genetic mutations, environmental factors, or both. Maternal cigarette smoking is strongly associated with cleft lip and palate, and at least 26 genetic loci identified by GWAS contribute to the nonsyndromic form, highlighting a combined genetic-environmental (multifactorial) etiology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No trisomy is described here; chromosomal abnormalities are one intrinsic cause of anomalies but do not explain this multifactorial phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A deformation results from mechanical forces reshaping a normally formed structure; cleft lip arises from failure of tissue fusion during development.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autosomal recessive inheritance describes NECTIN1-related CLPED1, a syndromic form; nonsyndromic cleft lip with palate involves many loci plus environmental factors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Smoking is strongly associated with clefting, but the many GWAS loci show a genetic contribution as well, so the cause is not purely environmental.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman is exposed to a significant dose of a chemical teratogen at week 24 of gestation, well after all major organs have formed. Which of the following is the most likely consequence for the fetus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amputation of digits from amniotic band formation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of the conceptus as the only possible outcome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Major structural anomalies from disrupted organogenesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minor structural changes or functional deficits

choices.label: E
choices.text: No possible effect because development is complete

explanation.summary: Exposure during weeks 9-38 most often causes minor structural changes or functional deficits.
explanation.whyCorrect: Weeks 9-38 constitute a less sensitive period because organogenesis is largely complete. Teratogenic exposure during fetal development is therefore more likely to cause minor structural changes or functional deficits rather than major structural anomalies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amniotic band injury is a mechanical disruption caused by torn strands of amniotic tissue, not the expected effect of a chemical teratogen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of the embryo as part of an all-or-none effect characterizes exposure during weeks 1-2, before significant differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Major structural anomalies result from exposure during weeks 3-8, when organogenesis is occurring, not at week 24.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The fetal period is less sensitive, not insensitive; minor structural and functional abnormalities can still occur.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 27-year-old pregnant woman has an entirely asymptomatic primary infection with a TORCHeS pathogen during the first trimester. Her fetus is later found to have multiple congenital anomalies. Which of the following best explains how fetal injury occurred despite the absence of maternal symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: External mechanical forces compressed the developing fetus

choices.label: B
choices.text: High maternal phenylalanine acted as a metabolic teratogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ionizing radiation damaged rapidly dividing embryonic cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Placental vasoconstriction reduced oxygen delivery to the fetus

choices.label: E
choices.text: The pathogen crossed the placenta despite subclinical maternal illness

explanation.summary: Maternal infection may be mild or asymptomatic, yet the pathogen can still cross the placenta and injure the fetus.
explanation.whyCorrect: During pregnancy the maternal immune system is relatively suppressed, increasing susceptibility to certain pathogens. Importantly, maternal infection may be mild or even asymptomatic, yet the pathogen can still cross the placenta and affect the fetus, which is what makes the TORCHeS organisms clinically dangerous.

whyWrongByChoice.A: External mechanical forces produce deformations such as clubfoot; they do not explain anomalies following a maternal infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Elevated phenylalanine crossing the placenta is the mechanism of maternal phenylketonuria, a maternal metabolic condition, not an infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DNA damage in rapidly dividing cells is the mechanism of ionizing radiation, a physical teratogen, and is unrelated to this infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Placental vasoconstriction is the mechanism by which cocaine causes low birth weight and prematurity, not how an infection injures the fetus.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: The TORCHeS acronym summarizes the classic infections that can be transmitted in utero. Which of the following pathogens is grouped under the "Other" category of this acronym?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rubella virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Toxoplasma gondii

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zika virus

explanation.summary: The "Other" agents in TORCHeS include parvovirus B19, varicella-zoster virus, Listeria, HIV, and Zika virus.
explanation.whyCorrect: In TORCHeS, the "O" stands for Other agents, which include parvovirus B19, varicella-zoster virus, Listeria monocytogenes, HIV, and Zika virus. The remaining letters each name a specific pathogen: Toxoplasma gondii, Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes simplex virus type 2, and Syphilis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytomegalovirus is the "C" of the acronym, with its own named position.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Herpes simplex virus type 2 is the "He" of the acronym, with its own named position.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rubella is the "R" of the acronym, with its own named position.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxoplasma gondii is the "T" of the acronym, not part of the Other group.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A newborn is found to have microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss, and impaired vision. Congenital infection with which of the following pathogens is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Listeria monocytogenes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parvovirus B19

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rubella virus

explanation.summary: Congenital CMV infection causes microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, hearing loss, and vision impairment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection may result in microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, hearing loss, and vision impairment. CMV is a TORCHeS pathogen that can cross the placenta even when the maternal infection is mild or asymptomatic.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Herpes simplex virus type 2 is a TORCHeS pathogen, but the combination of microcephaly, calcifications, hearing loss, and vision impairment is characteristic of CMV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Listeria monocytogenes is an "Other" TORCHeS agent transmissible in utero, but it is not linked to this constellation of findings.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parvovirus B19 is one of the "Other" TORCHeS agents; it is not the pathogen associated with this pattern of microcephaly and calcifications.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Congenital rubella classically causes cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease rather than microcephaly with intracranial calcifications.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has been taking an oral medication for severe acne. She learns she is 7 weeks pregnant. The fetus is at greatest risk for which of the following patterns of anomalies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Craniofacial, cardiac, and central nervous system anomalies

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve

choices.label: C
choices.text: Limb reduction defects of the upper and lower extremities

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neural tube defects of the lumbosacral region

choices.label: E
choices.text: Smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and joint anomalies

explanation.summary: Retinoic acid, used for severe acne, causes craniofacial, cardiac, and central nervous system anomalies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retinoic acid, used to treat severe acne, is a chemical teratogen that can cause craniofacial, cardiac, and central nervous system anomalies. Exposure at week 7 falls within the most sensitive period of organogenesis, compounding the risk.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve is associated with lithium, used for bipolar disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Limb reduction defects (phocomelia) are the hallmark of thalidomide exposure, not of an acne medication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neural tube defects are associated with valproic acid, which disrupts folate metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, and joint anomalies are features of fetal alcohol syndrome.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is treated for a malignancy with a medication that was originally marketed in the 1950s as a sedative and anti-nausea drug. She becomes pregnant during treatment. The fetus is at greatest risk for which of the following anomalies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cataracts with sensorineural deafness

choices.label: B
choices.text: Craniofacial and central nervous system anomalies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve

choices.label: D
choices.text: Limb reduction defects

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neural tube defects

explanation.summary: Thalidomide, a 1950s sedative and anti-nausea drug now used for certain cancers, causes limb reduction defects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thalidomide was originally used as a sedative and anti-nausea medication in the 1950s and is now used for certain cancers. It is a classic chemical teratogen known for causing limb reduction defects (phocomelia).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cataracts and sensorineural deafness are features of congenital rubella infection, an infectious rather than chemical teratogen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Craniofacial, cardiac, and central nervous system anomalies are the pattern caused by retinoic acid used for severe acne.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ebstein anomaly is associated with lithium, the mood stabilizer used in bipolar disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neural tube defects are associated with valproic acid, which disrupts folate metabolism, not with thalidomide.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A woman who smoked one pack of cigarettes daily throughout her pregnancy delivers a preterm infant with low birth weight. Which of the following mechanisms most likely underlies these outcomes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disruption of folate-dependent DNA synthesis in the embryo

choices.label: B
choices.text: DNA strand breaks in rapidly dividing embryonic cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fetal hyperglycemia with oxidative stress and free radicals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired placental blood flow with reduced oxygen delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transplacental passage of excess maternal phenylalanine

explanation.summary: Smoking causes low birth weight and preterm labor largely through impaired placental blood flow and reduced fetal oxygen delivery.
explanation.whyCorrect: Smoking during pregnancy is associated with low birth weight and preterm labor, largely due to impaired placental blood flow and reduced oxygen delivery to the fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Disrupted folate metabolism is the mechanism by which valproic acid raises the risk of neural tube defects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DNA strand breaks in rapidly dividing embryonic cells describe the injury caused by ionizing radiation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fetal hyperglycemia with oxidative stress is the mechanism of injury in poorly controlled maternal diabetes mellitus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenylalanine crossing the placenta is the mechanism of maternal phenylketonuria, a metabolic teratogen.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: An infant is born prematurely with low birth weight. There are no dysmorphic facial features, limb defects, or major structural anomalies, but during childhood he develops subtle intellectual and cognitive disabilities. Prenatal exposure to which of the following substances is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cocaine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lithium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thalidomide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Valproic acid

explanation.summary: Cocaine causes placental vasoconstriction, leading to low birth weight, prematurity, and subtle intellectual and cognitive disabilities.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cocaine can cause placental vasoconstriction, leading to low birth weight, premature delivery, and subtle intellectual and cognitive disabilities. The absence of characteristic facial features or structural anomalies distinguishes this pattern from other teratogenic exposures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Significant alcohol exposure causes fetal alcohol syndrome, with growth restriction, joint anomalies, heart defects, and characteristic facies such as a smooth philtrum, which are absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lithium is associated with Ebstein anomaly, a structural malformation of the tricuspid valve, which this infant does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thalidomide causes limb reduction defects, and this infant has no limb abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Valproic acid disrupts folate metabolism and raises the risk of neural tube defects, which are not present.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: In murine studies, chronic alcohol exposure in males before conception produces offspring with craniofacial abnormalities, including micrognathia and retrognathia, and at high doses disrupted facial symmetry and eye positioning. Which of the following mechanisms best explains how this paternal exposure alters offspring development?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A new activating point mutation in the paternal FGFR3 receptor gene

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depletion of maternal folate stores before conception occurs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct transplacental passage of alcohol to the developing embryonic tissues

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epigenetic modifications altering expression of key developmental genes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasoconstriction of the placental blood vessels with fetal hypoxia

explanation.summary: Paternal alcohol effects on offspring morphogenesis in mice are linked to epigenetic modifications regulating key developmental genes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic paternal alcohol exposure in mice leads to craniofacial abnormalities including micrognathia and retrognathia, highlighting the link between environmental factors and epigenetic modifications that regulate the expression of key genes during embryonic development. To date, this effect has not been demonstrated in human studies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FGFR3 mutation causes achondroplasia, a skeletal dysplasia with impaired endochondral ossification, not these paternal-exposure findings.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate status is a maternal factor relevant to neural tube defect prevention; it does not explain transmission of a paternal alcohol effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The exposure is paternal and occurs before conception, so alcohol cannot reach the embryo across the placenta as it does with maternal drinking.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Placental vasoconstriction is the mechanism of maternal cocaine use, causing low birth weight and prematurity.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: During early pregnancy, a woman is exposed to high levels of ionizing radiation. Radiation damages rapidly dividing embryonic cells, chiefly by causing DNA breaks. The fetus is at greatest risk for which of the following patterns of anomalies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and structural cardiac defects

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coloboma, choanal atresia, growth retardation, and genital anomalies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Constriction rings with amputation of digits and limb defects

choices.label: D
choices.text: Microcephaly, intellectual disability, cleft palate, and skeletal defects

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vertebral defects, anal atresia, and tracheoesophageal fistula with renal anomalies

explanation.summary: High-dose ionizing radiation can cause microcephaly, intellectual disability, cleft palate, and skeletal and visceral defects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ionizing radiation, such as from high-dose x-rays or nuclear exposure, damages rapidly dividing embryonic cells mainly through DNA breaks. High-level exposure during fetal development can affect multiple organ systems, causing microcephaly, intellectual disability, cleft palate, and various skeletal and visceral defects, with severity depending on both dose and timing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease constitute the classic pattern of congenital rubella infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coloboma, choanal atresia, and genital anomalies are features of CHARGE syndrome, caused by CHD7 mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Constriction rings and digital amputations result from amniotic bands, a mechanical disruption rather than a radiation effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vertebral defects, anal atresia, and tracheoesophageal fistula are hallmark features of the VACTERL association.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus throughout pregnancy delivers an infant with multiple congenital anomalies. Because maternal and fetal blood glucose levels correlate, the fetus experienced sustained hyperglycemia and oxidative stress. Anomalies of which of the following organ systems are most characteristic of this exposure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eyes, ears, and external genitalia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Limbs, digits, and amnion-adjacent skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lungs, urinary tract, and facial contour

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nervous system, skeleton, and heart

choices.label: E
choices.text: Palate, hair, and other ectodermal structures

explanation.summary: Poorly controlled maternal diabetes causes congenital nervous system, skeletal, and heart anomalies via fetal hyperglycemia and oxidative stress.
explanation.whyCorrect: In maternal diabetes mellitus, maternal blood glucose levels correlate with fetal blood glucose levels. Poorly controlled diabetes during pregnancy causes fetal hyperglycemia and oxidative stress, which can lead to congenital nervous system, skeletal, and heart anomalies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coloboma of the eye, ear abnormalities, and genital anomalies suggest CHARGE syndrome, a genetic disorder from CHD7 mutation, not diabetic embryopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Injury to limbs and digits with skin constriction describes amniotic band disruption, a mechanical process unrelated to maternal glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary hypoplasia, a urinary system defect, and flattened facies together describe Potter sequence, which begins with a primary urinary abnormality.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cleft palate with ectodermal dysplasia describes the NECTIN1-related syndrome CLPED1, not the pattern of diabetic embryopathy.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman planning her first pregnancy asks what she can do to reduce the risk of neural tube defects and craniofacial malformations in her child. Which of the following recommendations most directly addresses this risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Avoiding cigarette smoke during the third trimester only

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folic acid supplementation starting before conception

choices.label: C
choices.text: Radiation shielding during any x-ray imaging

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reliance on newborn screening to detect anomalies early

choices.label: E
choices.text: Screening for maternal diabetes during prenatal visits

explanation.summary: Folic acid before conception and through early pregnancy reduces the risk of neural tube defects and craniofacial malformations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Folic acid supplementation before conception and throughout early pregnancy is a cornerstone of prevention. It supports DNA synthesis and methylation, significantly reducing the risk of neural tube defects and craniofacial malformations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tobacco avoidance matters throughout pregnancy for birth weight and prematurity, and limiting avoidance to the third trimester would miss the critical early period anyway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Radiation shielding minimizes exposure to a physical teratogen but does not address the folate-dependent processes behind neural tube closure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Newborn screening, such as PKU testing, identifies conditions after birth; it does not prevent neural tube defects in the current pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diabetes screening helps prevent anomalies from fetal hyperglycemia; it is not the measure aimed specifically at neural tube defects.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: All newborns in the United States undergo screening for phenylketonuria shortly after birth. Which of the following best explains how this screening program helps prevent congenital anomalies in the next generation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It detects elevated phenylalanine in the fetus during gestation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It determines which mothers require folate supplementation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It enables dietary counseling before affected girls later become pregnant

choices.label: D
choices.text: It identifies which fetuses have inherited the enzyme defect

choices.label: E
choices.text: It screens embryos for the mutation before implantation

explanation.summary: Newborn PKU screening allows dietary counseling that prevents elevated maternal phenylalanine in future pregnancies.
explanation.whyCorrect: In maternal PKU, high phenylalanine levels cross the placenta and act as a metabolic teratogen, causing intellectual disability, heart defects, and intrauterine growth restriction. Because all newborns undergo PKU screening, affected individuals are identified early, so maternal dietary counseling can prevent elevated phenylalanine levels in future pregnancies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Newborn screening is performed after birth on the infant; it does not measure fetal phenylalanine during gestation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folate supplementation prevents neural tube defects; it is unrelated to the phenylalanine control that PKU screening enables.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The fetal risk in maternal PKU comes from exposure to the mother's elevated phenylalanine, not from whether the fetus inherited the enzyme defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Screening embryos before transfer describes pre-implantation genetic testing during IVF, a separate preventive strategy.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A couple at high risk of transmitting a single-gene disorder plans to conceive through in vitro fertilization. Which of the following strategies is most appropriate to reduce the chance of transferring an affected embryo?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Folic acid supplementation before conception

choices.label: B
choices.text: Newborn metabolic screening after delivery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pre-implantation genetic testing of the embryos

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prenatal surgical repair during gestation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Radiation shielding during maternal imaging

explanation.summary: Pre-implantation genetic testing during IVF detects chromosomal abnormalities and single-gene disorders before embryo transfer.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pre-implantation genetic testing during IVF helps detect chromosomal abnormalities and single-gene disorders before embryo transfer, offering families with high genetic risk the chance for healthier pregnancies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Folic acid reduces the risk of neural tube defects and craniofacial malformations; it does not detect or prevent a single-gene disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Newborn screening identifies conditions such as PKU after birth; it cannot influence which embryo is transferred.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prenatal surgery corrects selected structural anomalies such as spina bifida in utero; it does not prevent transmission of a genetic disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Radiation shielding limits exposure to a physical teratogen and has no role in screening embryos for an inherited mutation.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A fetus is diagnosed with spina bifida during the second trimester, and the family elects in utero surgical repair. Which of the following best explains the developmental rationale for correcting this anomaly before birth rather than afterward?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early repair prevents secondary complications cascading from the defect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intervention shortens the most teratogen-sensitive developmental window

choices.label: C
choices.text: Repair converts an intrinsic malformation into a minor deformation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgery during gestation restores depleted maternal folate stores

choices.label: E
choices.text: The operation corrects the underlying genetic cause of the anomaly

explanation.summary: Prenatal surgery for spina bifida prevents the secondary complications (sequence disorders) that follow the primary defect.
explanation.whyCorrect: In selected cases, prenatal surgery can correct structural anomalies like spina bifida in utero, preventing secondary complications (sequence disorders) and improving postnatal outcomes. Because a sequence is a cascade in which one abnormality leads to the next, interrupting the primary defect early stops downstream anomalies from developing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The teratogen-sensitive window of weeks 3-8 is determined by the timing of organogenesis and cannot be shortened by an operation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The classification of the original defect does not change with treatment; the goal is to block secondary complications, not to reclassify the anomaly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folic acid supplementation is a preconception and early-pregnancy preventive measure; fetal surgery has no effect on maternal folate status.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Surgery repairs the structural defect; it cannot change a genetic or other underlying cause of the anomaly.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A newborn has an isolated cleft lip. The pregnancy was uncomplicated, with normal amniotic fluid volume, no evidence of amniotic bands, and no intrauterine crowding. Imaging and pathology indicate that the facial tissues failed to fuse normally from the beginning of their development. This anomaly is best classified as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Association

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deformation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disruption

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dysplasia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Malformation

explanation.summary: Cleft lip from failure of normal tissue fusion is a classic malformation, an intrinsically abnormal developmental process.
explanation.whyCorrect: A malformation is a morphologic anomaly resulting from an intrinsically abnormal developmental process: the structure never forms normally because of an underlying problem in the developmental program, such as a genetic mutation or disrupted signaling pathway. Cleft lip, arising from failure of normal tissue fusion, is a classic craniofacial malformation, as are congenital heart defects associated with chromosomal abnormalities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An association is a pattern of multiple co-occurring anomalies without a unifying cause, not a single isolated defect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A deformation reflects external mechanical forces reshaping intact tissue; amniotic fluid volume was normal and there was no crowding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A disruption requires an extrinsic force damaging a structure that was developing normally, such as amniotic bands; here no external insult occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dysplasia is disorganized cellular architecture within a tissue; cleft lip is a failure of an entire structure to form, not a tissue-level organization defect.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A second-trimester ultrasound shows a normally forming fetal organ. Weeks later, occlusion of the vessel supplying that organ occurs, and the organ subsequently develops abnormally. Which of the following best classifies the resulting anomaly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deformation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disruption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dysplasia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Malformation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Syndrome

explanation.summary: Loss of blood supply to a normally developing organ causes a disruption.
explanation.whyCorrect: A disruption is an extrinsic breakdown or interference with a structure that was developing normally. Beyond amniotic bands, disruptions also include teratogens that damage normally forming structures at the time of exposure and loss of blood supply to a developing organ, which causes it to develop abnormally.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A deformation is caused by mechanical forces that alter shape or position while tissue remains intact; ischemic injury damages the developing tissue itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dysplasia is an intrinsic genetic abnormality of cellular organization within a tissue, not the consequence of an acquired vascular insult.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A malformation requires an intrinsically abnormal developmental program from the outset; this organ was documented to be forming normally before the vascular event.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A syndrome is a group of anomalies arising in parallel from one underlying cause, not a single organ injured by loss of its blood supply.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: Malformations and dysplasias are both intrinsic errors of morphogenesis. Which of the following features most reliably distinguishes a dysplasia from a malformation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dysplasia arises only after teratogenic exposure in late gestation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dysplasia describes anomalies cascading from one initiating event

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dysplasia involves disorganized cellular architecture within a tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dysplasia is caused by external mechanical forces on the fetus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dysplasia results from extrinsic interruption of normal development

explanation.summary: Dysplasia is abnormal cellular organization within a tissue, whereas a malformation is failure of an entire structure to form normally.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dysplasia is an intrinsic developmental abnormality characterized by disorganized cell structure within a tissue, typically from genetic mutations that alter cell growth, differentiation, or signaling. A malformation, by contrast, affects the formation of an entire structure from the beginning; the distinction is the level at which development goes wrong.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dysplasias typically arise from genetic mutations, not from teratogenic exposure late in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A cascade of anomalies from a single initiating event defines a sequence, such as Potter sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: External mechanical forces acting on normally developing tissue define a deformation, not a dysplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Extrinsic breakdown of a normally developing structure defines a disruption; dysplasia is intrinsic.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A newborn is found to have vertebral defects, anal atresia, and a tracheoesophageal fistula. Chromosomal analysis is normal, there was no teratogenic exposure, and an extensive evaluation identifies no single unifying cause for the anomalies. This pattern is best classified as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Association

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deformation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dysplasia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sequence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Syndrome

explanation.summary: VACTERL is an association: findings that co-occur more often than expected without an identified unifying cause.
explanation.whyCorrect: An association is a group of findings that occur together more often than expected, but with no single unifying cause identified. This infant meets criteria for VACTERL association (Vertebral defects, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects, Tracheo-Esophageal fistula, Renal anomalies, Limb abnormalities), which is often sporadic and requires at least 3 of the hallmark features for diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A deformation is a single anomaly of shape or position caused by mechanical forces, not a multi-organ pattern of malformations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dysplasia is disorganized cellular architecture within one tissue, not a constellation of anomalies across organ systems.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A sequence is a cascade in which one abnormality leads to the next, as in Potter sequence; these anomalies did not arise from a single initiating defect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A syndrome requires a single underlying cause, such as a chromosomal abnormality or gene mutation, and none was identified here.

questions.topicName: Errors in Morphogenesis

questions.stem: A term newborn fails to pass meconium and develops severe constipation. Rectal biopsy shows absence of ganglion cells in the distal colon, and genetic testing identifies a mutation in the RET proto-oncogene. Which of the following developmental processes was most directly impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Closure of the neural tube in early gestation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endochondral ossification of developing cartilage

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of adherens junctions in epithelia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fusion of the facial tissues at the midline

choices.label: E
choices.text: Migration of enteric neural crest cells

explanation.summary: RET mutations impair enteric neural crest cell migration, causing Hirschsprung disease with absent colonic ganglion cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mutation in the RET proto-oncogene impairs migration of enteric neural crest cells, leading to Hirschsprung disease with absence of ganglion cells in the colon and severe constipation. Because neural crest cells migrate to and differentiate into diverse tissues, including craniofacial structures, peripheral nerves, melanocytes, and parts of the heart, a single defect in their development can affect multiple organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Failure of neural tube closure causes neural tube defects, associated with folate disruption, not absence of colonic ganglion cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Impaired endochondral ossification results from FGFR3 mutation in achondroplasia, producing skeletal dysplasia rather than aganglionosis of the colon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defective adherens junction formation from NECTIN1 mutation causes cleft lip/palate with ectodermal dysplasia, not Hirschsprung disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failure of facial tissue fusion produces cleft lip, a craniofacial malformation unrelated to colonic innervation.
